newsitem.title: UK: LME aluminium puts in demand as market weakens.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium puts in demand as market weakens.

text.p: Aluminium options business picked up on the London Metal Exchange (LME), with large tonnages traded earlier in the week as underlying three month futures plunged to 2-1/2 year lows.
Covering of $2,000 copper call options for October was also seen as market makers squared up ahead of the next options declaration on October 2.
"On Tuesday we saw particularly good business on aluminium. There was good buying around for puts in the last quarter of 1996 and the first quarter of 1997," said one dealer.
"This is the first time we have seen good aluminium turnover for some time," said another.
The strikes traded ranged from $1,350 to $1,450.
There were differing views over who was behind the buying, although several dealers agreed the business included a good amount of covering by market-makers short forward options.
"What I saw was covering," said one. "We saw volatilities for these puts trading at 18 and 18.50 percent."
"The covering was of volatility, because people have been short of 1997 exposure the whole time," another added.
Some traders said U.S. producers were also getting some downside protection on board.
"There has been a bit of U.S. producer business involved," said an options trader.
"The producers presumably did not expect to see the market get down this far," said another.
Traders said short-covering and producer interest still did not explain the size of the tonnages involved.
On Tuesday LME data showed over 11,000 aluminium puts traded, equating to more than 280,000 tonnes.
Call business that day exceeded 4,000 lots.
Some dealers said the put buying could have been part of an effort to push outright aluminium prices lower.
"It could be something of a game to get people to look downwards," said one. "Buying puts is an easy way to focus people's attention on the downside."
By midday Friday aluminium was looking vulnerable to more downside pressure. Futures were at fresh lows of $1,403, and any break below $1,400 could trigger more sell stops, traders said.
Granting into renewed demand was free, and volatilities in fact eased slightly over the week.
This reflected the widely held view that volatilities were overvalued, particularly for forward options in 1997.
October volatility was quoted at around 16.50 percent early on Friday, down a point on week-ago levels. November volatility eased around 0.75 of a percentage point and December 0.50.
First quarter 1997 volatility fell to around 17.50 percent from 18 percent on Monday.
Copper business focused on covering of October $2,000 calls, with traders keen to avoid a repeat of the expensive covering operation during the run-up to the September expiry.
Market makers said the risk which options posed to underlying market stability was slowly being eroded as books were squared both to the upside and downside.
"The further we go on the less risk there is on people's options books," said one trader.
Talk this week of continued U.S. producer put granting and buying by investment banks short of these positions supported this view.
"I don't think they (the banks) are square yet, but they are in a better position than they have been," a trader said.
Dealers said producer interest was emerging for forward min-max strategies in late 1997, involving selling of upside calls and buying of downside puts.
Copper option volatilities were little changed over the week, with October steady at 29 percent, and November and December a touch lower at 28.50 and 27.50 percent respectively.
Average 1997 volatility was quoted at just over 23 percent.
Activity in other base metal options was light and mixed, but volatilities for all were little changed on the week.
